title: Welcome banner
brief: Read a name and an age from the keyboard, then print a greeting that predicts next year's age.
hint: Scanner reads text with nextLine(); joining text and values in println needs the + operator.

blanks.explanation: new creates a Scanner object and invokes its constructor with System.in as the input source.
A name is text, and Scanner.nextLine() returns a String rather than a numeric value.
nextLine reads the whole name line, including spaces. The parentheses are already supplied after the gap.
Both operands are integers here, so + adds one to age to calculate nextYear.
The left operand is already a String. Here + concatenates nextYear with the greeting instead of performing numeric addition.

steps: Create a Scanner, read the name as a full line, then read the age as an integer. The text read happens before nextInt(), so there is no leftover numeric-input newline to consume here.
Calculate nextYear by adding one to the entered age, then concatenate the name and nextYear into the greeting.
The prompts and greeting depend on the supplied input; the checker neither requests console input nor runs this program.

title: Average mark
brief: Total three marks, compute a decimal average, and print it to two decimal places.
hint: Divide by 3.0 to perform floating-point division; assigning total / 3 to a double would still truncate first.

blanks.explanation: Add all three marks to obtain 227. This gap expects quiz + midterm + finalExam; reordered but equivalent sums are not listed as accepted answers.
total / 3.0 produces a double, so average needs a floating-point type. Using double alone would not fix integer division if both operands were integers.
/ divides the total by the number of marks. The double literal 3.0 makes this floating-point division, preserving the fractional part.
printf interprets %.2f as a floating-point value with two digits after the decimal separator and %n as a platform line break.
Math.round(double) returns the nearest long value; this average rounds to 76. round is the method name, with its argument already outside the gap.

steps: The sum is 78 + 64 + 85 = 227. Dividing by 3.0 gives approximately 75.6667, rather than the truncated integer result 75.
printf formats the average to two fractional digits; the decimal separator follows the default locale, so a single locale-independent output transcript is not shown.
Math.round returns 76, which is concatenated with the Rounded label. Formatting to two places and rounding to an integer are different operations.

title: Grade classifier
brief: A nested if/else chain turns a score into a grade letter, including an A+ tier.
hint: Java has no elseif keyword: the second branch is written as two words.

blanks.explanation: if tests the score once and enters the top grade branch when score is at least 80. A while loop would repeatedly test an unchanged score.
This else belongs to the inner if. Reaching it means score is at least 80 but below 90, so the grade is A.
else if adds a condition only after the score >= 80 branch failed. Here it selects scores from 70 through 79; Java spells it as two separate keywords.
>= includes the boundary score 50. Earlier branches already handled scores of 70 or more, so this branch covers 50 through 69.
Fail must be a double-quoted String literal. Without quotes it would be a name; single quotes are for a single character, not a word.

steps: Check the largest threshold first. Scores of at least 80 enter the nested test, which separates A+ (90 or more) from A (80 through 89).
Only a failed outer test can reach the B branch; after that, the inclusive threshold 50 selects C and the final else selects Fail.
The result depends on the entered score. This example does not reject scores outside an intended 0-100 range.

title: Drink menu with switch
brief: A switch picks a menu item; then a conditional operator labels the choice as valid or not.
hint: Use break to avoid fall-through from Coffee or Tea. The fallback is default, and the conditional operator is ? :.

blanks.explanation: switch selects a branch by comparing the integer choice with case labels. The surrounding case syntax belongs to a switch, not an if.
case 1: labels the branch for choice equal to 1. The numeric value and colon are already supplied.
break exits the switch after Coffee, preventing fall-through into Tea and Water while still allowing the label code below to run.
default handles every value not matched by cases 1 or 2. It prints Water for 3 and for out-of-range choices; case 3 alone would not cover those other values.
The conditional expression uses condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. Choices 1 through 3 produce valid; all others produce invalid.

steps: Read the integer choice. Cases 1 and 2 print Coffee or Tea and break out of the switch without falling through.
The default branch prints Water for all other choices, not just 3. For example, 4 would print Water and then invalid; the switch itself does not validate the range.
The separate conditional expression checks both inclusive bounds and chooses valid or invalid. Output therefore depends on input.

title: Sum and average to n
brief: Accumulate 1 to n with a for loop, then print the total and a decimal average.
hint: Start the accumulator at 0, keep looping while i <= n, and cast before dividing.

blanks.explanation: Zero is the neutral starting value for addition: the total must contain only values added by the loop, with no initial offset.
The loop must include n itself. With i starting at 1, <= visits every integer from 1 through a positive n; < would omit the final value.
i++ updates the loop variable by one after each iteration. i + 1 only describes a value and does not assign it back to i.
sum += i adds the current i to the accumulated total. = would replace the total, while == compares values rather than accumulating them.
Casting sum to double before / promotes the division to floating point. Casting the result of integer division afterward would be too late to recover a fractional part.

steps: For a small positive n, start sum at zero, add i for each i from 1 through n, and increment i after each addition.
The printed average divides the double-converted sum by n, preserving fractions. Both printed values depend on input.
This example assumes a positive n and totals that fit in int. It has no input guard: n = 0 produces NaN in the floating-point division, and sufficiently large totals can overflow.

title: Nested multiplication table
brief: Two nested loops print a 3 by 3 table and add every product to a running total.
hint: The inner loop finishes one row; the outer loop prints the line break. Use += to accumulate.

blanks.explanation: Increment row after each complete inner loop. row++, row += 1 and row = row + 1 are all explicitly accepted ways to move to the next row.
col begins at 1 and must visit 1, 2 and 3 in every row. <= 3 includes the third column.
Multiply the current row and column to obtain the cell value. Multiplication happens before concatenation with the trailing space.
+= keeps a running sum of all nine products. Using = would retain only the last product rather than the total.
The no-argument println() writes a line break after the inner loop, placing the next row on a new line.

steps: For each row from 1 to 3, restart col at 1 and print the three products. Each product is followed by one space.
The row totals are 6, 12 and 18, so the accumulator ends at 36.
println() ends each row, then the final statement prints the total. The worked transcript retains the trailing space on each table row.

title: Average until sentinel
brief: Keep reading numbers until the user types 0, then print the average only if something was entered.
hint: A sentinel loop tests the value before entering the body; count the values so you can divide safely.

blanks.explanation: while tests the value before each iteration, so an initial zero skips the body. The first value is read before this test.
Increase count once per nonzero value added to total. Each listed increment form is accepted, and the terminating semicolon is already present.
if (count > 0) allows division only after at least one data value was counted, avoiding a zero denominator for the empty-input case.
else handles the only remaining case, count equal to zero, and prints No values entered without needing another condition.
!= means not equal in Java. Continue while value is not the zero sentinel, which is excluded from both total and count.

steps: Read one integer before testing the sentinel. Each nonzero value contributes to total and count, then the next value is read inside the loop.
Zero ends the loop without contributing to either accumulator. Negative nonzero numbers are data too.

If at least one value was counted, calculate a floating-point average; otherwise print No values entered. The result depends on the input sequence, assuming it ends with zero and the int accumulators do not overflow.

title: Bank account
brief: A small class with a private field, a constructor, a getter, a deposit method, and a main that uses them.
hint: this.balance names the current object's field; opening is the constructor parameter used to initialize it.

blanks.explanation: The constructor and deposit method accept double values, and getBalance returns double, so this example stores balance as double too.
this.balance explicitly selects the current object's field. The parameter is named opening, so plain balance would also be valid Java here, but only this.balance is an authored answer.
return sends the field's value back to the caller of getBalance(), fulfilling the method's double return type.
A deposit increases the existing balance by amount, so the assigned expression is balance + amount.
new BankAccount(50.0) creates an account and calls the constructor with an opening balance of 50.0.
deposit(25.0) invokes the instance method that adds to the balance. The getter would only read the balance and takes no argument.

steps: Construct an account with opening equal to 50.0 and assign that value to the private balance field.
Calling deposit(25.0) changes the same object's balance to 75.0. getBalance() then returns that value to println.
This is a field-and-method example, not a production banking model: it permits negative deposits and uses floating-point rather than exact decimal money arithmetic.

title: Rectangle methods
brief: Instance methods compute area and perimeter; a static helper doubles another rectangle's area.
hint: A static method belongs to the class, so you call it as Rectangle.doubleArea(r).

blanks.explanation: A rectangle's area is width multiplied by height. Here the fields are doubles, so the expression matches area()'s double return type.
The perimeter expression uses double fields and returns a double. int would require a narrowing conversion, and void would forbid returning a value.
The surrounding expression already multiplies by 2, so this gap adds width and height inside the parentheses to form 2 * (width + height).
r.area() calls the instance method on rectangle r, using that object's width and height.
Rectangle.doubleArea(r) calls the static helper through the class name and passes the object whose area should be doubled.

steps: The constructor stores width 3.0 and height 4.0 in r. Its instance methods return area 3.0 * 4.0 = 12.0 and perimeter 2 * (3.0 + 4.0) = 14.0.
The static doubleArea helper receives r as an argument, calls r.area(), and returns 24.0 without changing the rectangle.
main prints the three returned values in order, with their labels.

title: Animal and Dog
brief: Dog extends Animal, calls the parent constructor, and overrides speak(); main calls the override through an Animal reference.
hint: A subclass reaches the parent constructor with super(...), and @Override documents the override.

blanks.explanation: Creating a Dog gives pet an actual Dog object even though the reference type is Animal. This sets up dispatch to Dog's overridden speak method.
speak() is the instance method declared on Animal and overridden by Dog. Calling it through pet uses the implementation for the actual object.
A class extends another class. implements is used for interfaces, not for inheriting from the Animal class.
super(name) calls Animal's constructor to initialize the inherited name field. Animal has no no-argument constructor, so the name must be passed explicitly here.
@Override asks the Java compiler to check that speak really overrides an inherited method. The annotation documents and checks intent; it does not itself cause dynamic dispatch.

steps: Construct Dog with Rex and pass the name to Animal's constructor using super(name).
Store the Dog object in an Animal reference. Calling pet.speak() still selects Dog's override based on the object's runtime class.
Dog.speak() returns Woof; the stored name is not included in this method's return value.

title: Shape polymorphism
brief: An abstract Shape is implemented by Circle and Square; a loop prints each area through the parent type.
hint: An abstract method has no body and must be implemented by a concrete subclass.

blanks.explanation: Shape declares an abstract method with no body, so the class must be abstract. Concrete subclasses provide the implementation and can be instantiated.
The code already supplies Math.PI *. Multiplying radius by itself completes the circle-area formula pi times radius squared.
A square's area is side squared, expressed as side * side, not twice the side or zero.
This array initializer creates a radius-2 circle and a side-3 square in that order. Both are Shapes, so they can share a Shape[] array.
shape.area() invokes the override for each array element. The loop can use the common Shape type without testing whether the element is a Circle or Square.

steps: Shape defines the abstract area contract. Circle and Square implement it using their own dimensions.
Create the array in circle-then-square order. Dynamic dispatch gives approximately 12.5664 for the circle and 9.0 for the square.
printf displays each area on its own line with two fractional digits. The decimal separator depends on the default locale, so no locale-independent transcript is supplied.

title: Login window
brief: Build a small Swing window: a frame, a panel, a label, a text field, and a button.
hint: Components are added to a container with add(), and the frame is given a size before it is shown.

blanks.explanation: import makes the javax.swing.JButton type available by its simple name JButton in this source file.
JFrame.EXIT_ON_CLOSE is the defined close-operation constant that requests application exit when this frame is closed.
panel.add(label) places the label in the panel's component hierarchy, alongside the text field and button added below.
setSize accepts width and height, here 320 by 160. pack() instead sizes from preferred component sizes and takes no arguments.
setVisible(true) requests that the frame be shown. false hides it, and the numeric value 1 is not a Java boolean.

steps: Create a frame and a panel, then add the username label, text field and sign-in button to the panel in that order.
Add the panel to the frame, choose a close operation, set the frame size and make it visible. The button has no listener here, so this is a layout example, not a working login.
No console output or live window is produced by this lab checker. In a real Swing application, schedule GUI creation on the event-dispatch thread.

title: Grid of buttons
brief: Use GridLayout to place six buttons in two rows, then show the frame.
hint: GridLayout takes rows then columns; add() places each component in the next cell.

blanks.explanation: GridLayout(2, 3) arranges these six components in two rows and three columns with equally sized cells.
Increment i once after each button is added, so the loop creates exactly six buttons labelled 1 through 6. All three listed increment forms are accepted.
The String operand Button followed by a space makes + concatenate the current integer i into the button label.
frame.add(button) adds the new component to the frame's content pane, where its GridLayout assigns the next cell.
Passing the boolean true to setVisible requests display after the buttons, size and close operation have been configured.

steps: Install a GridLayout before adding components. The loop creates Button 1 through Button 6 and adds them in numerical order.
With the default left-to-right orientation, the first three buttons occupy the first row and the next three the second row. Set the size and close operation before requesting visibility.
This is a worked layout, not a rendered Swing preview or console transcript. Real Swing GUI creation should be scheduled on the event-dispatch thread.

title: Click counter
brief: Register an anonymous ActionListener that counts clicks and updates a label.
hint: A JButton fires ActionEvent, so the listener must implement actionPerformed(ActionEvent).

blanks.explanation: addActionListener registers the anonymous ActionListener with the button so it receives action events when the button is activated.
ActionListener's callback is named actionPerformed and takes an ActionEvent. Matching that signature implements the interface method.
clicks++ increases the instance field by exactly one for each action event, before the updated number is read for the label.
JLabel.setText replaces the label's displayed text with Clicks: followed by the newly incremented count.
frame.setVisible(true) requests display of the configured frame. This gap needs the full method call; the statement semicolon is already supplied.

steps: Construct the frame, button and initial Clicks: 0 label. Register the anonymous listener before showing the window.
Each button action would invoke actionPerformed, increment clicks and replace the label text. clicks is an instance field, so it can be updated inside the listener.
The label changes depend on user actions; the lab does not simulate clicks or execute Swing. In a real app, create the GUI on the event-dispatch thread, where Swing action callbacks normally run.

title: Lambda greeting
brief: Replace the anonymous class with a lambda that opens a message dialog.
hint: ActionListener is a functional interface, so a lambda can supply its single abstract method.

blanks.explanation: static void main completes the conventional public static void main(String[] args) entry point: a class-level method with no return value.
addActionListener accepts an ActionListener, a functional interface that this one-parameter lambda can implement for button actions.
The -> token separates the event parameter from the lambda body. The following braces form a block body containing the dialog call.
JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(frame, message) shows a message dialog using frame as its parent component.
The button constructor needs a String label. Both double-quoted Say hello and Hello are authored answers; their label text does not change the dialog's message.

steps: Enter main, construct the frame and a button using either accepted label, and register the action-listener lambda.
Registration does not immediately open the dialog. A later button action would invoke the lambda and request a dialog containing Hello from Swing.
The example configures and shows the frame but has no console output. The checker does not open a window; real Swing setup should be scheduled on the event-dispatch thread.

title: Safe divide
brief: Parse two numbers inside try, catch a bad number and a divide-by-zero separately, and always run finally.
hint: Integer.parseInt throws NumberFormatException for invalid integer text; integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException.

blanks.explanation: try encloses the parsing and division operations whose exceptions the following catch clauses can handle.
catch introduces a handler with an exception type and a parameter named error. It runs only if an exception of the matching type reaches it.
Integer.parseInt throws NumberFormatException when a line is not a valid in-range integer representation, including text that is numeric but too large for int.
The operands a and b are ints. Integer division by a zero b throws ArithmeticException; floating-point division by zero behaves differently.
finally prints Done after successful division or after either shown handler. It is cleanup flow, not another conditional branch; JVM termination can prevent finally from running.

steps: Read and parse two lines in the try block. Successful nonzero-divisor integer division truncates toward zero and prints the quotient.
Invalid integer text takes the NumberFormatException handler; a parsed zero divisor takes the ArithmeticException handler instead. The failing operation skips the remaining statements in try.
The finally block prints Done on each of these paths. Which earlier line appears depends on input; exhausted input is a separate exception not caught by these handlers.

title: Withdraw guard
brief: Create a checked exception, throw it when the balance is too low, and catch it in main.
hint: A checked exception extends Exception, passes its message to super, and must be declared with throws.

blanks.explanation: Extending Exception directly defines a checked exception type. Exception is a class, so the inheritance keyword is extends, not implements.
super(message) passes the text to Exception's constructor, making it available later through the inherited getMessage() method.
throws in the method signature declares that withdraw can let InsufficientFundsException escape. Callers must catch this checked exception or declare it themselves.
throw raises the new exception object and exits the normal withdrawal path. It differs from throws, which only declares an exception on a method signature.
try encloses the call that may throw the checked exception, allowing the following catch to handle it and print the stored message.

steps: Construct the account with balance 100.0, then request a withdrawal of 150.0 inside try.
Because 150.0 exceeds 100.0, withdraw throws InsufficientFundsException before the subtraction. The balance remains 100.0.
The matching catch retrieves the message passed through super and prints Not enough money. This guard does not cover negative withdrawal amounts.
